DOCUMENT:
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone" -- 99 students x £9,250 = £915,750, about £0.9 million, not £1.2 million.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation." -- Students opted in, and the document reports mentees were more likely to live in halls (78% vs 52%) and to have higher entry qualifications, both associated with continuation. Self-selection and these confounders mean the gap does not show that mentoring caused higher continuation.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in" -- Scaling to 4,100 students at eight mentees per mentor needs about 513 mentors, but the document reports the University could fill only 155 of 200 advertised posts. The recommendation and costing assume mentor supply scales and never address the stated recruitment constraint (nor that automatically enrolled students may benefit less than volunteers).

REVIEW:
# Review of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Evaluation

The headline conclusion, that the scheme works and pays for itself many times over, is not supported by the evidence in the report. Some of the numbers are also wrong or cannot be right as stated.

## Major problems

**1. The 8-point gap is not evidence of a causal effect (selection bias).**
- Mentees opted in, and places went to those who took them up in the first two weeks. This favours the more engaged and motivated students.
- Section 3 shows the groups differ on factors known to predict continuation. 78% of mentees lived in halls versus 52% of others, and mentees tended to have higher entry tariffs.
- The report says the groups were "similar" on age and gender, which are the least relevant variables. It makes no adjustment for the differences that matter, such as regression controlling for halls, tariff, faculty, and prior engagement.
- The non-mentored group's 86% is below last year's overall figure of 87%. This is consistent with the more committed students having self-selected into the scheme, though it doesn't prove it.
- Calling this "clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation" is an overclaim. The data show an association only.
- There is a better comparison available. The 300-name waiting list contains students who wanted a mentor but didn't get one. Comparing mentees with that group would reduce the motivation bias considerably.

**2. The outcome data cannot be "complete" as described.**
- The report is dated July 2026 and claims to track students "through to the start of their second year". The second year hasn't started by July.
- The "continuing" figures must therefore be something else, such as re-enrolment intentions, progression decisions, or pre-registration. These are not the final enrolment census.
- The author's claim of "complete and objective" outcome data needs to be checked. The report should state exactly when and how continuation was measured.
- Even if the data were complete, objectivity of measurement doesn't fix the confounding in point 1.

**3. The financial arithmetic is wrong.**
- 99 students × £9,250 is about £916,000, not £1.2 million. £1.2m would need roughly 130 students.
- The pilot return is therefore about 4 times cost (£916k / £216k), not "several times" or "many times over" as the conclusion says. That is still positive if the effect were real.
- The 99 figure assumes the whole 8-point gap is causal. It also treats fee income as pure gain, ignoring the marginal cost of teaching and supporting those students. It counts only the second year, but then calls this "alone" without modelling later years either way.

**4. The roll-out costing and benefit are unsound.**
- The £174 per mentee is a pilot average. It does not scale simply to 4,100 students.
- The pilot struggled to recruit: 155 of 200 posts were filled. At 1:8, covering 4,100 students needs about 513 mentors, over three times the number recruited. The report never addresses whether this is feasible, or what higher pay or wider recruitment would cost.
- Coordination and training costs will not scale linearly either.
- The claimed benefit of "around 94% across the whole cohort" assumes an effect measured on self-selected volunteers applies equally to students who would not have opted in. Automatic allocation changes engagement, and the effect is likely smaller.
- The gain of "over 200" students (about 230) rests on that same assumption. The recommendation's benefits are therefore likely overstated while its costs are likely understated.

## Further issues

- **Satisfaction data:** The 4.3/5 rating gives no response rate, and students who left before the survey cannot have responded. It shows mentees liked the scheme, not that it affected continuation. "Consistent comments" are anecdotal and unquantified.
- **Year-on-year comparison:** The rise in overall continuation from 87% to 88.4% is a single-year change with no consideration of other factors, and cannot be attributed to the scheme.
- **Mentor outcomes:** Improved confidence and employability are self-reported, with no data shown.
- **Tone:** Phrases such as "large by any standard" and "one of the best-evidenced student success initiatives we have run" are not justified by an uncontrolled observational comparison.

## What I'd recommend before this goes forward

1. Confirm exactly how and when continuation was measured, and update the figures with the actual census data.
2. Compare mentees with the waiting-list group, and run an adjusted analysis controlling for halls residence, tariff, faculty, and other available covariates.
3. Correct the fee-income calculation, and present a range of effect sizes (for example, a half or a quarter of the raw gap) with sensitivity analysis.
4. Cost the roll-out around a realistic mentor supply, including recruitment, pay, and coordination at scale.
5. Consider a phased expansion, ideally with randomised or staggered allocation, rather than moving straight to automatic allocation for all 4,100 students.
6. Report the survey response rate.

The scheme may well help, but the report as written cannot show how much. Its financial case is mathematically off, and the recommendation rests on assumptions it doesn't test.
